claims.statement: Poland had approximately 11,762 publicly accessible charging points at the end of 2025, 36% more than a year earlier, including about 4,400 DC points.

The live EIPA registry listed 701 registered entities on 2026-08-24 and exposes legal names, CPO and/or mobility-provider identifiers, city, country, website, and registration date; this is a concrete top-of-funnel list, not a count of 701 addressable 20-500-connector fleets.
Registered EIPA readers can download separate JSON files for operators, charging pools, stations, points, and dynamic data, with operator contact fields and identifiers linking the asset hierarchy.

EIPA's documented dynamic record contains price, a binary operational-availability field, a free-or-busy field, and timestamps; access requires registration and is rate-limited, and UDT disclaims responsibility for the timeliness of operator-provided registry data.

AFIR Article 20 requires public-point operator/owner contact and identifiers plus operational status, availability, and ad-hoc price to be available through free, unrestricted APIs and national access points.

Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/655 requires static changes to be reflected within 24 hours, dynamic changes within one minute, source-side quality controls, and DATEX II formatting from 14 April 2026; it also requires Member States to monitor and address persistent data-quality problems.

The AFIR/EIPA layer can support fleet mapping and outage-led prospecting, but public out-of-order signals do not establish a separate reliability-operations budget or prove who has authority to buy outside an existing CPO, backend, installer, or OEM contract.

The public feed is not a diagnostic feed: its documented state fields cannot identify whether a failed charging attempt came from grid power, physical damage, safety protection, cellular connectivity, the backend, RFID, payment or authorization, vehicle handshake, power electronics, or connector locking.

Open Charge Alliance says the CPO is best positioned to attribute failures because successful charging depends on the station, CSMS, mobility/payment partners, app or card, and vehicle; OCPP alone is a message protocol and is not responsible for uptime.

When the station remains online and the service operator has authorized CSMS access, OCPP 1.6 and 2.0.1 provide useful remote actions including reset, connector unlock, status trigger, logs/diagnostics, firmware update, availability change, and configuration or variable reads/writes.

It is unknown what share of Polish mixed-brand fleets can grant a third party concurrent or replacement CSMS access, remote-command permission, diagnostic logs, payment evidence, and firmware rights without breaching backend, cybersecurity, warranty, or finance contracts.

ABB reports that customers on its own connected-services platform have 60% of service cases solved remotely, but that OEM-specific figure does not establish a cross-brand remote-close rate for an independent desk.

ABB bundles 24/7/365 monitoring, remote updates, troubleshooting, defined remote and on-site response stages, spare-parts coordination, and warranty service, and says repairs are exclusively performed by ABB-certified personnel or customer-selected personnel trained and certified by ABB.

A peer-reviewed field test of 655 US public DC fast-charging ports found 73.3% functional and observed screen/error, payment, initiation, network, and connector failures; its result conflicted with providers' reported 95-98% uptime. This demonstrates a measurement gap but is not Polish fault-frequency evidence.

GreenWay already markets in Poland an end-to-end business offer covering deployment, continuous monitoring, user management, settlement, servicing, reporting, and 24/7 operational support from single sites to large fleets.

Warsaw-based EVia Charge already markets essentially the proposed vendor-neutral offer: OCPP 1.6/2.0 multi-brand integration, connector-level monitoring, automatic fault detection, billing, 24/7 technical support, on-site support, and individually quoted SLAs.

A transparent European software benchmark is inexpensive relative to a managed service: E-Flux lists EUR 5.50 per AC socket/month and EUR 10.40 per DC socket/month and includes issue alerts plus remote reset and connector unlock.

Polish charging stations are subject to UDT technical examination before operation and after repair or modernization, with documentation review, inspection, and possible functional or load tests; UDT states a complete application is handled within 30 days.
No reviewed source establishes a recurring Polish budget for an independent reliability desk that is separate from CPMS, CPO-management, installer, warranty, or OEM service contracts.

EIPA identifies the responsible legal operator but does not identify the internal economic buyer; depending on ownership and contracts, authority could sit with a CPO operations lead, property/facilities owner, fleet manager, procurement, installer, financier, or OEM service owner.

No authoritative evidence found quantifies Polish technician density, travel radius and call-out cost, spare-parts lead time, after-hours burden, mixed-brand first-time-fix rate, or UDT-driven return-to-service delay for the target fleet segment.

A founder with at most five hours per day can plausibly run a business-hours 30-50-connector pilot, but cannot personally promise the 24/7 monitoring and response already marketed by direct competitors; scaling requires paid on-call coverage and field capacity before it creates software-like economics.

A research pricing case of PLN 120 per connector/month with a PLN 6,000 account minimum could produce a planning gross margin of roughly 35-45% only if field labor, travel, parts, and UDT costs are passed through and human incident time remains low; no source validates that price or workload.

Under the founder snapshot definition and without double-counting distributions, a conditional path to PLN 5 million of founder net worth requires about 4,700 connectors at PLN 120/month, 25% EBITDA, a debt-free 3.5x EBITDA value, and 85% founder ownership; that is about 40% of Poland's entire 2025 public-point base and therefore requires major market growth, CEE expansion, or incumbent displacement that current evidence does not support.

AFIR provides free and unrestricted access to the specified public data, but commercial storage, enrichment, cold-outreach use of EIPA contact data, and reuse of non-public OCPP, session, warranty, and repair records still require documented contractual and privacy rights.

The mixed-brand remote-close rate and the combined remote-or-one-visit-close rate remain unknown; ABB's 60% remote figure is not transferable, and neither public status data nor OCPP documentation supplies a Polish denominator.

contrary_evidence: The closest identified Polish competitor, EVia Charge, already advertises the same vendor-neutral OCPP monitoring, billing, remote support, on-site support, and tailored-SLA bundle. [evidence: S9]

GreenWay sells a larger end-to-end CEE bundle with continuous monitoring, settlement, service, reporting, and 24/7 operations, allowing property and fleet owners to buy from one established counterparty. [evidence: S8]

OEM service can already combine warranty, proprietary diagnostics, remote fixes, certified field personnel, parts, and response commitments; ABB says 60% of its connected service cases are resolved remotely. [evidence: S7]
The basic monitoring and remote-control software layer is price-compressed: E-Flux publishes EUR 5.50 per AC socket/month and EUR 10.40 per DC socket/month. [evidence: S12]

OCPP standardization makes reset, unlock, status, logs, firmware, and configuration functions portable enough to reduce software differentiation, while vendor-specific error fields and access rights preserve integration work rather than a clean moat. [evidence: S6]

EIPA's public status is binary and its publisher disclaims timeliness; even a legally improved one-minute feed is not proof that a driver can successfully initiate and complete a charge. [evidence: S3, S5, S10]

Warranty certification, spare-parts availability, physical travel, and UDT return-to-service steps constrain remote and one-visit closure and require an operating network rather than just monitoring software. [evidence: S7, S11]
The sources show a reliability problem but no separately appropriated Polish buyer budget; pain and public outage visibility cannot be treated as paid behavior. [evidence: S7, S8, S9, S10, S12]

unknowns: How many of the 701 EIPA-registered entities are Polish CPOs with 20-500 connectors, how many are only mobility providers, and how many assets are already managed under GreenWay, another CPO, a CPMS vendor, an installer, or an OEM SLA.
The named internal buying role, annual budget owner, procurement path, and signature authority for reliability operations in each ownership arrangement.

Current annual spend per connector on CPMS, monitoring, hotline, preventive maintenance, corrective maintenance, warranty extension, parts, and field call-outs, and which line items can actually be displaced.
The share of target chargers on OCPP 1.6, 2.0.1, proprietary protocols, or closed backends, plus whether a third party can receive safe production credentials or an OCPP proxy connection.
The share of current OEM, installer, finance, and CPMS contracts that permit third-party remote commands, firmware changes, logs, and repairs without voiding warranty or reallocating liability.
Polish mixed-brand incident frequency and fault mix by AC/DC, age, manufacturer, payment stack, connectivity type, and site environment.
Remote-close rate, remote-diagnosis rate, one-visit-close rate, repeat-fault rate, and false-positive rate measured on the same connector and ticket denominators.
Technician and OEM-authorized technician density by region, travel and call-out prices, on-call premiums, parts stocking requirements, and parts lead times.
Whether the one-minute AFIR data-quality rules are consistently implemented and audited across Polish operators in production, rather than only specified in law.
The commercial reuse, retention, enrichment, outreach, and derived-report terms applicable to EIPA downloads, and the controller/processor roles for non-public charging-session and repair data.
Real acquisition conversion from an outage report to a meeting, contract-data disclosure, prepaid pilot, and annual contract, including sales-cycle length and CAC.
Whether any buyer will prepay at least PLN 6,000/month for 50 connectors while field labor, travel, parts, OEM escalation, and UDT costs remain pass-through.
Whether a business-hours pilot can prove value without promising 24/7 coverage, or whether the relevant buyers categorically require 24/7 support from launch.
A credible valuation multiple for a labor- and field-service-dependent private operator, net of debt, working capital, customer concentration, warranty exposure, and key-person risk.
